source_title: San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance — chameleon
facts: A chameleon can aim its two eyes at different objects at the same time.
Chameleon colour changes can communicate mood and reproductive state, not just provide camouflage.
A chameleon cannot copy any colour or pattern it happens to sit on.
A chameleon's toes form opposing grasping bundles for gripping branches.
Many chameleons use their tails like an extra anchor when climbing.
A chameleon cannot shed and regrow its tail the way some other lizards can.
Chameleons catch insects with rapidly launched, sticky-tipped tongues.
Jackson's chameleons give birth to live young rather than laying eggs.
Male Jackson's chameleons can lock horns in contests on branches.
Namaqua chameleons live in the Namib Desert and shelter in sand to escape temperature extremes.

source_title: San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance — komodo dragon
facts: Komodo dragons are the largest living lizards.
Komodo dragon skin contains small bony plates that act as armour.
Young Komodo dragons climb trees to escape predators.
Komodo dragons sometimes use abandoned bird nesting mounds to incubate their eggs.
Female Komodo dragons may dig decoy nest chambers that confuse predators.
Komodo dragon mothers guard their nests for the first months after laying.
Wild Komodo dragons live on a small group of Indonesian islands.
Komodo dragons use burrows both as cool daytime shelters and for warmth at night.
Female Komodo dragons may skip breeding years to recover the energy spent producing eggs.
Komodo dragons can detect scents with their forked tongues.

source_title: San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance — crocodilian
facts: Crocodilians are more closely related to birds than to lizards.
Crocodiles can replace lost or worn teeth repeatedly throughout their lives.
Crocodilian mothers can hear young calling from inside their eggs.
Some crocodilian mothers gently carry hatchlings to water in their mouths.
Crocodilians may gape their mouths to release excess heat.
A crocodile's visible fourth lower tooth can help distinguish it from an alligator.
Crocodiles have salt-excreting tongue glands that help them tolerate salty water.
Sensitive organs in crocodilian skin detect movement in murky water.
Incubation temperature influences whether some crocodilian hatchlings are male or female.
Male gharials use the bulb on their snouts to help make courtship sounds.

source_title: San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance — snake
facts: Snakes cannot blink because they lack movable eyelids.
Some tree snakes flatten their bodies and glide between trees.
Sea snakes use flattened tails to propel themselves through water.
Egg-eating snakes break shells internally and spit out the remains.
Some snakes detect warm prey using specialised heat-sensitive pits.
A snake's jaw bones are loosely connected, allowing it to swallow unusually wide meals.
Some pythons generate warmth for their eggs through shivering muscle contractions.
Not all snakes lay eggs; some give birth to live young.
Snakes can shed their outer skin inside out, rather like removing a sock.
Spitting cobras spray venom as a defence rather than as their normal way of hunting.

source_title: San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance — frog and toad
facts: Toads are included within the broader group of frogs.
Touching a toad does not give you warts.
Some poison frogs obtain defensive chemicals from their natural insect diet.
Frogs can absorb oxygen and water through their skin.
A waxy tree frog spreads a water-saving coating over its body.
Some desert frogs burrow underground to survive dry conditions.
Fire-bellied toads can display brightly coloured undersides to warn predators.
Some male frogs carry eggs or tadpoles to safer places.
Frogs have distinctive mating calls that help females recognise their own species.
A tadpole's tail is absorbed into its body as it develops into a frog.

source_title: San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance — turtle and tortoise
facts: A turtle cannot leave its shell: the shell is joined to its ribs and spine.
Turtles can feel pressure and pain through their shells.
Some turtles fold their necks sideways rather than pulling them straight back.
Turtles have hard beaks instead of teeth.
Leatherback turtles have flexible, leathery shells rather than rigid plated ones.
Some freshwater turtles absorb oxygen through tissues near the rear of their bodies.
Nest temperature influences the sex of hatchlings in many turtle species.
Sea turtles can migrate thousands of kilometres and return to familiar nesting beaches.
A turtle may hiss simply by expelling air as it withdraws into its shell.
The freshwater Fly River turtle has flippers resembling those of sea turtles.

source_title: San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance — axolotl
facts: An axolotl is a salamander that normally keeps juvenile features throughout adulthood.
Axolotls retain feathery external gills rather than losing them as they grow up.
Axolotls can regrow lost limbs, including bone, muscle, and nerves.
An axolotl can use lungs as well as gills to obtain oxygen.
Wild axolotls are usually dark, unlike the pale pink individuals familiar from captivity.
Axolotls capture small prey by sucking it into their mouths.
Axolotls lay individual eggs on underwater objects such as plants and rocks.
Axolotl hatchlings receive no parental care after hatching.
Axolotls' natural home is the freshwater wetland system of Mexico's central valley.
Conservation refuges in Xochimilco use barriers to keep introduced fish away from axolotls.
